case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government may treat a returning lawful permanent resident as an applicant for admission under INA § 101(a)(13)(C)(v) based on proof (including post-entry evidence) that the LPR has committed an offense identified in INA § 212(a)(2), even if the conviction was entered after the LPR’s return.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) (returning LPR treated as seeking admission if he “has committed an offense identified in” 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)); 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) (inadmissibility for crimes involving moral turpitude); related removal provisions and burdens of proof in removal proceedings (including 8 U.S.C. § 1229a and implementing regulations, as implicated by the parties’ burden arguments).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that Congress adopted a conduct-based framework in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v): a returning LPR can be treated as seeking admission if he has in fact committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense, and the government may rely on evidence that becomes available after the LPR is paroled/let in (such as a subsequent conviction) to prove that prior commission. The government contends the Second Circuit erroneously required conviction-level proof at the time of entry (or otherwise constrained the government to the border record), undermining Congress’s design for border integrity and public safety and making § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) difficult to administer.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Lau argues that the government cannot retroactively convert his prior return to the United States into an ‘application for admission’ based on later-developed evidence, and that the government failed to carry (or even properly litigate) the applicable burden to establish a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception. He also contends the case is a poor vehicle because removability ultimately turns on a separate merits question—whether his trademark counterfeiting offense qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude—and because the government allegedly forfeited any challenge to the clear-and-convincing standard by accepting that standard before the agency and the Second Circuit.
key_precedents: Doe v. Attorney General, 659 F.3d 266 (3d Cir. 2011) (discussed regarding the burden of proof for § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions and the court supplying a standard absent precedent)

Board of Immigration Appeals precedent referenced by the parties as establishing that the government must prove a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception by clear and convincing evidence (specific case name not provided in the excerpts)
Second Circuit decision below, 130 F.4th 42 (Pet. App. 1a-15a) (the decision under review)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s structural “retroactive conversion” concern is serious, but it ultimately depends on adding a time-of-entry evidentiary constraint that § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) does not contain. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statute asks whether the returning LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—conduct-based language that is naturally proven, when disputed, in the later § 1229a removal proceeding Congress provided, not frozen to what happened to be known at the port of entry. Nothing in the text requires a conviction at reentry, and § 1182(a)(2) itself is not uniformly conviction-dependent, confirming Congress did not make admissibility classification hinge on contemporaneous documentation. We can keep the holding narrow: post-return proof (including a later conviction) is not categorically barred from establishing pre-return commission, while leaving burdens, evidentiary weight, and any agency framework questions for remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “retroactive conversion” concern rests on an atextual premise that § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) is limited to what DHS knew or could prove at the port of entry. The statute instead asks whether the returning LPR “has committed” an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2), and as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain, that cross-referenced provision is not uniformly conviction-dependent—confirming Congress chose a conduct-based trigger rather than a conviction-at-entry rule. As Justice Barrett notes, Congress designed § 1229a proceedings as the forum for determining whether an exception applies, with the Government bearing the burden; using a later conviction as evidence of pre-return commission fits that structure without collapsing inadmissibility and deportability. With a detailed, enumerated scheme, I see no warrant for importing lenity or a “time-of-entry proof” limitation Congress did not write.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “retroactive conversion” argument has force rhetorically, but it depends on reading into § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) a temporal/evidentiary limitation Congress did not enact. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Congress chose conduct-based language—an LPR is treated as seeking admission if he “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and § 1182(a)(2) itself is not uniformly conviction-dependent, which undercuts any conviction-at-entry rule. The INA’s structure anticipates that whether an exception in § 1101(a)(13)(C) applies will be determined in § 1229a proceedings, where later-developed evidence can prove earlier conduct; treating a post-return conviction as proof does not “collapse” tracks so much as apply the statutory trigger Congress specified. Lenity cannot justify adding an atextual carveout to a carefully enumerated scheme, especially in this domain of political-branch control over admission procedures.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett are right that § 1101(a)(13)(C) contemplates litigation of the exception in later § 1229a proceedings, and that “has committed” is conduct-based language. But that framing does not answer my structural concern: allowing post-return proof to newly place an LPR on the inadmissibility track risks untethering clause (v) from the admission decision Congress set up and invites the Government to bypass the deportability track’s calibrated burdens and protections by relabeling what is functionally a post-entry removal case. Section 1101(a)(13)(C) is a narrow carveout from the presumption that returning LPRs are not seeking admission, and absent clearer textual direction that Congress authorized this backward-looking conversion based on later-developed evidence (here, a conviction post-dating return), lingering ambiguity should be resolved in the noncitizen’s favor. I therefore remain unpersuaded by Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s view that there is “nothing in the text” to tie the inquiry to the time of reentry; the statute’s two-track structure supplies that limiting context.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s retroactivity concern is the best argument on the other side, but it asks us to graft onto § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) a temporal/evidentiary limitation Congress did not write. The clause turns on whether the LPR “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2)—a conduct-based trigger—and, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, Congress placed the adjudication of that predicate in later § 1229a proceedings with the Government bearing the burden, making post-return evidence (including a later conviction) a means of proving an earlier fact, not a device for changing the legal framework after the fact. Nor does this collapse inadmissibility and deportability: § 1101(a)(13)(C) itself defines when a returning LPR is treated as seeking admission, and our job is to apply that definition according to its plain terms. Absent textual support for a “known at the border” or “conviction at entry” requirement, I would not invent one under the banner of structure or lenity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “retroactive conversion” concern presses on a real structural feature of the INA’s inadmissibility/deportability divide, but the text Congress chose in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) makes the trigger the pre-return fact that the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—not the Government’s state of knowledge or the port-of-entry record. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, importing a conviction-at-entry or contemporaneous-proof limitation would add an atextual carveout to an enumerated list, effectively turning an evidentiary question into a timing rule Congress did not enact. The statutory scheme anticipates that these predicates are litigated in later § 1229a proceedings under assigned burdens, where later-created documents (including convictions) can serve as evidence of earlier commission without collapsing the tracks. On that understanding, respondent’s rule looks less like faithful interpretation and more like a judicially implied exception, and I do not see statutory signals sufficient to justify it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the structural worry about “retroactive conversion” of an effectuated reentry into an application for admission, potentially blurring inadmissibility and deportability. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) is written in status-and-conduct terms—an LPR is treated as seeking admission if he “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and nothing in that text limits the Government’s proof to what was known or documented at the port of entry or requires a conviction at that moment. The later conviction does not change the operative historical fact; it is simply evidence that the pre-return commission occurred, to be tested in § 1229a proceedings under the assigned burdens. Reading in a time-of-entry evidentiary restriction would add an atextual carveout to Congress’s tightly enumerated 1996 framework and create arbitrary outcomes driven by border happenstance rather than statutory predicates.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s structural concern about “retroactive” relabeling is serious, but the text and structure she invokes point the other way: § 1101(a)(13)(C) sets a rebuttable presumption and specifies six exceptions, and Congress directed that those predicates be adjudicated in § 1229a removal proceedings with the Government bearing the burden. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, clause (v) turns on whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—conduct-based language that is not naturally read to impose a conviction-at-entry or port-of-entry-record limitation, especially given that § 1182(a)(2) is not uniformly conviction-dependent. Treating a post-return conviction as evidence of pre-return commission does not collapse inadmissibility and deportability tracks; it simply supplies proof in the forum Congress selected for deciding whether an exception to the LPR presumption applies. Imposing a temporal/evidentiary restriction absent from the statute would add an atextual caveat to a carefully enumerated scheme, and I do not see lenity doing that work where Congress’s allocation of decisionmaking and review is this explicit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “retroactive conversion” concern is substantial, but it asks us to graft onto § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) a temporal/evidentiary limit Congress did not write. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1101(a)(13)(C) is structured to have its exceptions adjudicated in § 1229a removal proceedings under assigned burdens, and nothing in clause (v)’s conduct-based trigger (“has committed”) confines the Government to the port-of-entry record or to convictions already obtained at reentry. The cross-reference to § 1182(a)(2)—which is not uniformly conviction-dependent—confirms that Congress keyed the inquiry to commission, not to the timing of proof; a post-return conviction can be probative of a pre-return fact without collapsing inadmissibility and deportability into one. Because respondent’s limiting rule would require inferring a silent constraint that the statute does not “answer . . . directly,” I remain with petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: The enacted text asks whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in” § 212(a)(2); it does not say “has been convicted,” and we do not lightly assume Congress omitted a conviction-at-entry requirement it supposedly intended to impose. Reading § 101(a)(13)(C)(v) as conduct-based also fits the cross-reference, because § 212(a)(2) includes grounds that can turn on conduct rather than a conviction, and importing a temporal limitation barring post-entry proof would add an unstated caveat that conflicts with the ordinary meaning of “committed.” On these facts, the Government may rely on a later conviction as evidence that the offense was in fact committed before the return, while leaving for the agency on remand (under ordinary burdens of proof in removal proceedings) whether the Government can carry its burden and whether the offense qualifies under § 212(a)(2). Any contrary suggestion in Vartelas is dicta and “hedged,” and the Court can resolve this case narrowly on the statutory text without rewriting it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2), and Congress chose a conduct-based predicate (“committed”), not a conviction-at-the-border requirement; nothing in the operative text limits the Government to the evidentiary record as it existed at the moment of inspection. Reading such a temporal/evidentiary restriction into this detailed, enumerated scheme would add an atextual exception to Congress’ carefully cabined list of circumstances when an LPR is treated as seeking admission. On these facts, the Government may rely on later-developed proof—such as a post-return conviction—to establish that Lau in fact committed the § 212(a)(2) offense before his return, and the separate question whether his particular offense is a CIMT goes to the merits of inadmissibility, not to the threshold statutory authority to treat him as an applicant for admission. To the extent respondent invokes reliance interests or “retroactivity” concerns, IIRIRA’s replacement of Fleuti with § 1101(a)(13)(C)’s categorical framework forecloses importing equitable gloss that would narrow Congress’ border-scrutiny design.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s text and structure make the returning LPR’s status turn on whether he “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2), a conduct-based trigger that Congress used to define when an LPR is treated as an “applicant for admission” under § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v). Nothing in that provision limits the government to evidence available at the moment of inspection; allowing post-return proof (including a later conviction) to establish prior commission fits Congress’s design to restore meaningful border scrutiny after Fleuti and avoids arbitrary disparities whereby an LPR who crosses the threshold a few feet inland would gain an anomalous procedural advantage over an otherwise identically situated arriving alien. Given Congress’s plenary authority over admission and exclusion and its power to specify “whatever procedure authorized by Congress” for those treated as seeking admission, the Second Circuit’s border-record/conviction-at-entry limitation is inconsistent with the statute’s administrable, parity-based scheme. The government therefore may treat Lau as an applicant for admission upon proving—by the applicable burden in removal proceedings—that he in fact committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense even if the conviction post-dated his return.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The INA’s post-IIRIRA two-track structure presumes a returning lawful permanent resident is not “seeking admission,” and § 1101(a)(13)(C) carves out narrow, enumerated exceptions that must be established in the admission context and in a manner consistent with the statute’s allocation of burdens. Reading § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) to allow DHS to retroactively convert an already-effectuated reentry into an “application for admission” based on later-developed evidence untethers inadmissibility from the admission decision Congress carefully structured and risks collapsing the inadmissibility/deportability divide by letting the Government relabel what is functionally a deportability case as an inadmissibility one. Given the textual and structural complexity—particularly Congress’s use of “admission” and its proxies—and the absence of clear language authorizing this backward-looking reclassification, any lingering ambiguity should be resolved under the immigration rule of lenity in the noncitizen’s favor. On these facts, where the conviction was entered only after the return, the Government has not shown that § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) properly applied at the time of Lau’s reentry to place him on the inadmissibility track.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns, by its plain terms, on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2)—language directed at the offense conduct, not at the existence or timing of a conviction at the port of entry. Reading the statute holistically, Congress created a presumption that an LPR is not seeking admission, but then allowed DHS to rebut that presumption in removal proceedings by proving one of the six enumerated exceptions; nothing in the text limits proof to the border record or bars reliance on later-obtained evidence (like a post-return conviction) to establish pre-return commission. That approach respects the INA’s term-of-art distinctions: the question here is whether the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception applies (a separate, independent prerequisite to treating the LPR as an applicant for admission), not whether later events can “cure” or redefine the LPR’s underlying status. So long as DHS carries its burden—typically by clear and convincing evidence—to show the LPR in fact committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense before the return, DHS may treat him as an applicant for admission even if the conviction comes later.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2), and Congress’s choice of “committed” signals a conduct-based inquiry rather than a conviction-at-the-border requirement. Nothing in the text supplies a timing carveout limiting the government to the port-of-entry record or forbidding reliance on later-obtained proof (like a post-return conviction) to establish that the offense was committed before reentry; recognizing such a restriction would add words Congress did not enact. Under the INA’s burden framework, the government must prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception in the removal proceedings, and the statute elsewhere anticipates evidentiary disputes resolved by documentary proof and credibility determinations—making post-entry evidence a routine, not anomalous, feature of adjudication. The Second Circuit’s rule effectively reintroduces a Fleuti-like insulation from border consequences for criminal conduct, contrary to IIRIRA’s restructuring of “admission” and its enumerated exceptions for returning LPRs.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The operative text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) asks whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2); it does not say “has been convicted” at the time of reentry, and Congress’s choice of the conduct-based verb “committed” triggers the admission-applicant status once the statutory condition is met. Because § 1182(a)(2) itself includes grounds that do not uniformly depend on convictions, the cross-reference functions as a deliberate trigger mechanism tied to the fact of commission, with a later conviction serving as admissible proof of that earlier conduct in removal proceedings. Reading the provision within Congress’s comprehensive 1996 scheme, the government’s ability to establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception at the time of adjudication (including with post-entry evidence) better fits the statute’s status-based design and avoids an administrability problem where border records alone would control. On these facts, DHS may treat Lau as seeking admission if it proves—by the applicable clear-and-convincing standard—that he committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense before his return, even though the conviction was entered afterward.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) asks whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2), which is conduct-based language and does not, by its terms, require that a conviction already exist at the moment of reentry. The INA’s structure assigns that determination to the removal-process institutions (DHS charging and IJ adjudication under § 1229a) with the government bearing the burden—under the BIA’s framework in Matter of Rivens—of proving a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception by clear and convincing evidence; a post-entry conviction is powerful evidence of prior commission and can satisfy that burden without rewriting the statute into a time-of-entry conviction requirement. Treating later-developed proof as admissible in the ensuing removal proceedings respects Congress’s allocation of decisionmaking and avoids converting an evidentiary question into an extra-textual temporal limitation on § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v). The Second Circuit’s rule effectively adds a border-record/at-entry constraint that the statutory text does not contain and that is difficult to square with the INA’s adjudicatory design.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text Congress chose in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v)—that a returning LPR is treated as seeking admission if he “has committed an offense identified in” § 1182(a)(2)—is conduct-based, not conviction-timed, and it contains no words limiting what evidence the Government may use or requiring that a conviction exist “at the time of entry.” Reading such a timing restriction into this stage-setting definition would add an atextual constraint Congress did not write, and it would sit awkwardly with the broader removal scheme in § 1229a, which contemplates that facts bearing on removability (including criminal conduct) may be proven in proceedings using evidence developed after the triggering event. The presumption for LPRs in § 1101(a)(13)(C) is real, but it is rebuttable; the Government may rebut it by proving—by whatever burden applies under the agency’s rules and the parties’ litigation positions—that the person in fact committed a § 212(a)(2) offense, and a later conviction can be probative proof of earlier commission. Nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) “answers directly” that DHS must decide the exception only on the contemporaneous border record, so the respondent’s proposed limitation would require the Court to infer a silent mandate that the provision’s words and structure do not supply.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government may treat a returning lawful permanent resident as an applicant for admission under the INA based on proof that the person committed a listed offense (including one involving moral turpitude) before reentry, even if the conviction (or conclusive proof) arises only after the person is paroled/allowed into the United States, and what evidentiary standard governs proving that exception.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), chiefly 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) (when an LPR is treated as seeking admission), 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2) (criminal grounds of inadmissibility, including crimes involving moral turpitude), related removal provisions in 8 U.S.C. § 1227, and burden-of-proof provisions applicable in removal proceedings (including the clear-and-convincing framework reflected in agency precedent and litigation positions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that Congress adopted a conduct-based admission framework for returning LPRs in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5): if the LPR has committed an offense described in § 1182(a)(2), the LPR falls within an exception and can be treated as seeking admission. Under that framework, DHS may rely on evidence establishing commission of the offense even if the case matures administratively after the person is permitted to enter/paroled (e.g., later-obtained disposition/conviction records), because requiring conviction-level proof at the border would undermine border screening and public-safety objectives. The government also takes the view that the respondent committed an offense (trademark counterfeiting) that qualifies under § 1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) and therefore he is properly chargeable and ineligible for the sought relief (including a § 212(h) waiver per the agency decisions).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the Second Circuit correctly held he was not removable on the government’s chosen theory because the government failed to prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception at the relevant time and under the required standard; the government cannot retroactively convert a returning LPR into an arriving applicant for admission based on post-entry developments. Respondent further contends that the governing burden to establish an exception stripping LPR protections is clear and convincing evidence (as reflected in BIA precedent the government accepted below), and that the government forfeited any attempt to argue for a lower burden in this Court. He also stresses vehicle problems: the question presented may not be outcome-determinative because removability ultimately hinges on whether his offense qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude—an issue the government did not ask the Court to decide.
key_precedents: Doe v. Attorney General, 659 F.3d 266 (3d Cir. 2011) (burden standard discussion for § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions; described as federal common-law gap-filling in the materials)
BIA precedent referenced by the parties as requiring the government to prove a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception by clear and convincing evidence (specific case name not provided in the excerpted materials)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas press the strongest textual point: § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) asks whether the LPR “has committed” a covered offense, and nothing expressly limits what later evidence may prove that historical fact. But that does not answer the antecedent structural question Congress posed in § 1101(a)(13)(C): the LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” an exception is established as a threshold, reentry-stage classification, and allowing DHS to admit the person and then later reclassify him as an arriving applicant turns that protective default into post hoc label-shifting. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, that reading collapses the INA’s staged scheme by letting the Government bypass § 1227’s post-entry removability track after it has already treated the return as non-admission. A narrow affirmance can accommodate the petitioners’ textual concern by leaving open the Government’s ability to use later-developed proof when it properly invokes clause (v) at the relevant stage, while rejecting retroactive conversion after admission has been permitted.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest point for Respondent—pressed by the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett—is the structural concern that § 1101(a)(13)(C) operates as a reentry-stage classification and thus cannot be “retroactively” altered once DHS has permitted return. But that objection depends on reading into clause (v) a timing-of-proof limitation Congress did not enact: the text asks only whether the LPR “has committed” an offense “described in” § 1182(a)(2), a historical fact that may be proven later in removal proceedings, as Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch explain, without transforming evidentiary development into “label-shifting.” The INA repeatedly contemplates that admissibility predicates and their proof will be adjudicated in § 1229a proceedings, and nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) “expressly and carefully” cabins the Government to the port-of-entry record. Absent clear statutory language imposing an evidentiary freeze or a heightened threshold burden, I would not graft such constraints onto Congress’s detailed scheme simply to avoid asserted structural discomfort.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett raise the best objection—§ 1101(a)(13)(C) is framed as a reentry-stage classification rule and they worry our reading would allow DHS to "relabel" status after permitting return. But that concern imports a timing-of-proof restriction Congress did not enact: clause (v) turns on the historical fact that the LPR "has committed" a covered § 1182(a)(2) offense, and later-obtained conviction records may prove that predicate without altering when it occurred, as Justices Thomas and Kavanaugh emphasize. Treating evidentiary timing as dispositive would reintroduce the very happenstance distinctions (how quickly records are found) Congress’s admission framework is designed to avoid, while the Government still must satisfy whatever burden applies in the ensuing removal proceeding. The INA’s structure separates substantive predicates from the mechanics of proof, and I do not read § 1101(a)(13)(C) to create an implicit port-of-entry evidentiary freeze.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas are right that the clause (v) text—“has committed”—is conduct-based and does not, on its face, impose a port-of-entry evidentiary freeze. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly identify the dispositive structural problem: § 1101(a)(13)(C) is a threshold, reentry-moment classification rule (“shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless”), and the Government’s reading turns that protective default into a revocable label that DHS can rewrite after it has already allowed the person to return. Later-developed records may prove historical conduct, but they cannot supply authority for a post hoc conversion from the deportability track Congress provided for post-entry consequences to the inadmissibility track, absent a clear directive. Given the severe real-world consequences of that instability for long-term residents and families, I would require the Government to establish that the exception applied at the time of return before treating the LPR as an applicant for admission.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is textual: clause (v) asks whether the LPR “has committed” a covered offense, and nothing there expressly cabins the Government’s proof to the port-of-entry record. But that reads clause (v) in isolation from the function § 1101(a)(13)(C) assigns it—an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” an exception is established as a threshold classification tied to the reentry event, not a label the Government may revise after it has already treated the person as not seeking admission. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, allowing post hoc reclassification collapses Congress’s distinct inadmissibility and deportability tracks: Congress provided post-entry consequences through § 1227, and it did not say that later-discovered evidence can retroactively convert a permitted return into an “application for admission.” Later-obtained records can prove historical conduct, but they cannot supply statutory authority for a retroactive track-switch absent clearer text—so Rivens’ burden framework and the statute’s structure control here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s structural concern about “post hoc relabeling” rightly highlights that § 1101(a)(13)(C) operates at reentry, but it still presupposes an evidentiary timing rule Congress did not enact. Clause (v) asks a historical question—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) or § 1229a(c)’s burden allocations freezes the Government to the port-of-entry record in later removal proceedings. As Justice Kavanaugh underscores, importing a stage-specific proof limitation would blur the statute’s distinct processes (admission versus removal) and collapse Congress’s separate treatment of “commission” and “conviction” by effectively demanding a conviction (or its equivalent) at inspection. The Government must still satisfy the applicable burden of proof in removal proceedings, and when the record is incomplete that shortfall cuts against the party bearing the burden—but evidentiary timing alone is not a statutory bar.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is structural: § 1101(a)(13)(C) is framed as a reentry-stage classification rule, and they worry that later-developed proof allows post hoc relabeling after DHS has permitted return. But the statute’s operative trigger in clause (v) is not what DHS knew at the port of entry; it is whether the LPR “has committed” an offense described in § 1182(a)(2)—a historical, conduct-based predicate that either was true or was not true at the time of return, regardless of when the Government later proves it. As Justice Gorsuch notes, importing an “evidence-frozen-at-inspection” limitation adds a timing-of-proof requirement Congress did not write and sits uneasily with the INA’s ordinary practice of adjudicating admissibility predicates in removal proceedings using later-obtained conviction records. The reentry protection remains meaningful because the Government still bears the burden to prove that the exception applied; evidentiary timing alone should not defeat the categorical consequence Congress attached to the predicate fact.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas are right that clause (v) turns on a historical fact—whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—and the text does not expressly freeze the Government to the port-of-entry record. But that point does not answer the antecedent statutory allocation of authority in § 1101(a)(13)(C): Congress made “seeking an admission” a threshold, reentry-stage classification (“shall not be regarded ... unless”), and allowing DHS to admit/parole and then later retroactively invoke inadmissibility treats that threshold as revocable at will, collapsing the separate inadmissibility and deportability tracks the Chief Justice identifies. Consistent with Rivens and the INA’s burden structure, the Government must establish—at the point it matters for placing the LPR on the inadmissibility track—that an exception applies; later-developed evidence may prove the historical fact, but it cannot cure an initial failure to invoke the proper statutory posture after return. So I remain with Respondent: absent a timely and adequately supported invocation of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v), DHS must proceed, if at all, under § 1227.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh (echoed by Justices Thomas and Gorsuch) is right that clause (v)’s “has committed” phrasing is conduct-focused and does not itself contain an evidentiary timing rule. But that point does not answer the distinct, structural question Congress posed in § 1101(a)(13)(C): whether, at the reentry juncture, the LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission unless” an exception applies—a threshold classification that determines which statutory track governs. Allowing DHS to permit return and later invoke clause (v) to treat the person as having been an applicant for admission is not merely using later proof to establish an old fact; it is using later proof to expand the Government’s authority to select a different track after the reentry-stage decision has already been made, collapsing the INA’s staged scheme that the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett identify. Absent a clear textual instruction authorizing that post hoc status conversion, the Government must proceed (if it can) under the post-entry removability framework rather than retroactively recharacterizing the entry.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) establishes the default rule that a returning LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless the Government proves one of the enumerated exceptions, and § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) turns on whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—not whether DHS later develops evidence sufficient to reclassify him after he has been allowed in. Reading the statute’s structure to permit DHS to parole or admit an LPR and only afterwards supply the determinative proof would effectively convert the exception inquiry into a post hoc mechanism that dilutes Congress’s chosen protections for LPRs at reentry, rather than applying the exception at the time it matters. Consistent with longstanding burden allocations in removal proceedings and agency precedent, the Government must establish the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception by clear and convincing evidence, and on this record that showing was not made at the relevant time based on mere charges or incomplete proof. Because the Government’s position would expand discretion beyond the statute’s scheme and relax a settled evidentiary safeguard without clear textual warrant, I would affirm for Respondent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) provides that a returning lawful permanent resident “shall be regarded as seeking an admission” if he “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” and Congress’s choice of “committed” (not “convicted”) in this detailed admission scheme is a conduct-based trigger that does not depend on whether a conviction record exists at the port of entry. Nothing in the INA “expressly and carefully” conditions the applicability of that exception on the timing of the Government’s proof at inspection, and the statute’s structure contemplates that admissibility questions may be resolved in later removal proceedings rather than conclusively at the border. Nor does the INA expressly impose a heightened, extra-textual burden like “clear and convincing evidence” to establish a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception; where Congress specified burdens elsewhere, courts should not add one by gap-filling, and the agency may proceed under the burdens Congress actually enacted for removal proceedings. Because respondent committed the relevant offense before reentry, DHS could treat him as an applicant for admission and prove that predicate in the ensuing proceedings even if conclusive documentation was obtained after parole.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s text, as amended by IIRIRA to constrain Fleuti-like avoidance of inspection, makes a returning LPR an “applicant for admission” if he “has committed” an offense “described in” § 1182(a)(2), § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v), and nothing in that language limits DHS to evidence available at the precise moment of inspection or parole. Reading the statute structurally, Congress tied the consequence (admission treatment and inadmissibility procedures) to the predicate fact (commission of the listed offense), and it would undercut that scheme to make admissibility turn on the happenstance of when conclusive records are obtained after reentry. Because Congress has plenary authority over admission and specified the procedures for those treated as seeking admission, the court should not graft an extra-statutory “border-only proof” limitation onto § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v). As for the evidentiary standard, the government must at least meet the burden Congress and longstanding practice impose in removal proceedings, but that burden is satisfied here if the later-obtained conviction/record evidence establishes that the respondent in fact committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense before reentry.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A lawful permanent resident’s ability to travel and return without being stripped of long-settled status is a core protection Congress preserved even after IIRIRA, and treating an LPR as an “applicant for admission” is a serious status-altering step that must be narrowly applied with attention to real-world consequences. Where the government allowed or paroled the resident into the country and only later assembled conviction or other conclusive proof, fairness and access to justice require that DHS bear a heightened burden—clear and convincing evidence—to show that the § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) exception applied at the time of reentry, not retroactively based on post-entry developments. Allowing post hoc conversion of an admitted/paroled LPR into an arriving applicant invites error and destabilizes families and communities, disproportionately harming vulnerable noncitizens who reasonably relied on their resident status when traveling. Because the government did not carry (and in any event accepted below) the clear-and-convincing standard for stripping those protections, the removability theory as charged cannot stand on this record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) begins from the baseline that a returning LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless the Government proves one of the enumerated exceptions; that structure makes the exception an independent, threshold condition the Government must establish in the removal proceeding. And § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) turns on whether the LPR “has committed an offense described in § 1182(a)(2),” a phrase Congress elsewhere treats as requiring conviction or an alien’s own admission of the essential elements—not a later-developed record used to retroactively recharacterize the person’s already-effectuated return as an “application for admission.” Given the INA’s careful separation of concepts (returning LPR status versus arriving applicant for admission) and the long-recognized protections for returning LPRs, the Government must carry a heightened burden to strip that status, properly framed as clear, unequivocal, and convincing evidence, and it cannot satisfy that threshold by post-entry developments alone. On these facts—where the Government’s theory depends on proving the exception only after parole/entry—the statute’s text and structure do not authorize treating respondent as an applicant for admission.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text Congress chose in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” not whether he had already been convicted at the port of entry; importing a conviction-at-the-border requirement would add a condition the statute does not supply and would collapse distinct INA concepts of “commission” and “conviction.” In removal proceedings, the government bears the burden to establish that a § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception applies, and under the agency’s controlling construction in Matter of Rivens that showing is made by clear and convincing evidence—meaning evidentiary gaps on whether the alien in fact committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense cut against DHS. On these facts, DHS may rely on later-obtained, statutorily recognized conviction records to prove that the offense predated reentry, because the relevant statutory question is the pre-entry conduct and Congress did not freeze the proof to what was available at inspection. The Second Circuit’s contrary rule effectively creates a timing limitation on the government’s proof and a border-stage conviction requirement that the INA’s text and structure do not contain.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The controlling text in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning lawful permanent resident “has committed” an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2), which is a conduct-based legal status triggered by the predicate facts, not by when the Government happens to obtain conviction records. Nothing in the INA limits the evidence in removal proceedings to what DHS knew at the port of entry; the statute contemplates that removability and admissibility are adjudicated in removal proceedings where evidence can be presented and weighed, and later-obtained conviction records may prove that the offense had been committed before reentry. Consistent with the statutory scheme, “inadmissibility” operates categorically once the predicates are met, and the Government may treat the LPR as an applicant for admission if it proves the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception in the removal proceeding. Under the Board’s framework, DHS must carry that burden by clear and convincing evidence in removal proceedings, but it need not have satisfied that standard at the border itself.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The statutory posture is admission, not deportation: under § 1101(a)(13)(C) an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless DHS proves one of the enumerated exceptions, including that the LPR “has committed” an offense described in § 1182(a)(2). In removal proceedings the Government bears the burden on threshold predicates that make the person chargeable as inadmissible rather than removable, and the Board has long applied a clear-and-convincing standard to § 1101(a)(13)(C) exceptions (Matter of Rivens), which aligns with the INA’s broader allocation of burdens in § 1229a(c)(3)(A) and the reduced procedural posture only once removability is established. On these facts, DHS paroled/allowed respondent in and only later relied on post-entry developments; absent clear-and-convincing evidence at the relevant time that he had in fact committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense, the Government cannot retroactively reclassify him as an arriving applicant for admission, and must instead proceed (if at all) under § 1227’s deportability framework. That limited, text-driven conclusion respects Congress’s allocation of authority over admission while enforcing the statute’s express protection for returning LPRs unless an exception is proved.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets out the narrow circumstances in which a returning LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission … unless” one of six exceptions applies, and that inquiry is triggered at the point of reentry/inspection—not later—so the Government’s theory that it can retroactively transform an admitted/paroled LPR into an “arriving” applicant based on post-entry developments asks the Court to extend the statute’s command beyond the event Congress specified. Congress knew how to assign continuing or post-admission consequences elsewhere in the INA (e.g., deportability grounds in § 1227), so reading § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) to authorize after-the-fact relabeling would create a silent mandate and collapse the INA’s stage-specific framework for admissibility versus removability. Even accepting that § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) is conduct-based (“has committed”), the Government still must prove the exception with the heightened protection traditionally afforded LPR status in removal proceedings; absent a clear textual directive lowering that burden, the clear-and-convincing standard governs and was not satisfied on this record at the relevant time. On these facts, the Government’s chosen charge fails because it depended on later-obtained proof to establish a border-stage exception and thereby bypassed the INA’s distinct post-admission removal scheme.
